title: Climate anxiety and pro-environmental behavior: Evidence from The Netherlands
content:
by Stefan Bogaerts, Manon Kleijn, Patrick Klaiber, John Bechara, Loes Abrahams, Bell Piyasinchai, Tom Junker, Maximilian Achim Friehs, Alejandro Dominguez-Rodriguez, Kim Janssens, Marija Janković

This study investigates the association between climate anxiety and pro-environmental behavior, while accounting for general psychological functioning, resilience, loneliness, and demographic characteristics in Dutch population. Both linear and potential curvilinear associations were explored, given inconsistent findings in previous research. We hypothesized that climate anxiety would be positively associated with pro-environmental behavior and would explain unique variance beyond other factors. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 285 participants aged 18–85. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed to test the incremental contributions of climate anxiety (linear and quadratic terms), general psychological functioning (stress, depression, and anxiety), resilience, loneliness (social and emotional), and demographic characteristics (gender, age, and education) in pro-environmental behavior. The full model explained 44.1% of the variance in pro-environmental behavior. Climate anxiety was a strong and consistent factor, accounting for a substantial increase in explained variance (ΔR² = .371, p < .001). The association was linear rather than curvilinear. General psychological complaints, resilience, and loneliness did not explain additional variance once climate anxiety was included. Demographic variables such as gender and education, were initially associated with pro-environmental behavior but were no longer significant after accounting for climate anxiety, while age was not significant in any model. Climate anxiety appears to be positively associated with pro-environmental behavior and may represent a context-specific motivational factor. These findings suggest that climate-related concern, when accompanied by actionable pathways, may support engagement in sustainability behavior, although causal conclusions cannot be drawn.
